Endocrinology · published research

Radiation-induced thyroid dysfunction

One study found improved proliferation and thyroid-marker measures in irradiated thyroid cells and mice after near-infrared LED exposure. There is no clinical evidence in patients receiving radiation therapy.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

One study found improved proliferation and thyroid-marker measures in irradiated thyroid cells and mice after near-infrared LED exposure. There is no clinical evidence in patients receiving radiation therapy.

Summary of the Evidence

One Korean publication directly addresses radiation-induced thyroid dysfunction. It combines an in-vitro experiment using irradiated human thyroid cells with an ionizing-radiation mouse model. These are linked components of one paper, not two independent publications or clinical studies. No patient trial or separate replication is identified in the exact category.

Human and clinical evidence

No clinical study in people treated with radiation for thyroid disease or nearby cancers was identified. The cell line used in the laboratory is human-derived but does not count as a human treatment study.

Animal evidence

In mice exposed to radiation, 850-nm near-infrared LED treatment restored thyroid-tissue proliferation and improved measured thyroid-associated markers, including cAMP, thyroglobulin, TSH, T3, and T4, compared with radiation-only conditions. This is a favorable result in the tested animal model, not evidence that PBM prevents or reverses hypothyroidism in patients (Yoo et al. 2021).

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

In irradiated N-Thy-3.1 human thyroid cells, PBM improved survival and proliferation and affected p53, retinoblastoma-protein, cAMP, and thyroglobulin measures. The study tested 2, 5, and 10 J/cm², with 2 J/cm² producing the strongest cell-cycle response among the tested doses. These assays come from the same publication as the mouse experiment.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The study used 850-nm near-infrared LED light. Cultured cells received 2, 5, or 10 J/cm², while the mouse protocol is reported at 120 J/cm². The database does not provide a direct dose comparison that identifies the best exposure for an intact thyroid. The cell and mouse doses should not be treated as interchangeable, and external animal dosing cannot define a human treatment schedule.

Interpretation

The single study found improved cellular proliferation and recovery of several thyroid markers in irradiated cells and mice. It provides a favorable preclinical result, while leaving clinical effectiveness, duration, and safety during cancer radiotherapy unanswered. Independent replication is needed before applying the finding to patients.

Evidence strength in source summaryVery low for thyroid-marker recovery in preclinical radiation-injury models
Publications and records1 article

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

One publication reported recovery of thyroid-cell and thyroid-marker measures in irradiated cultured cells and mice. These findings point in a favorable direction within two linked models, but they come from a single study and no patient outcomes were measured. Independent replication, testing for tumor-related safety, and then carefully designed clinical studies would be needed to support a treatment claim.
